cases.case_name: Sheboygan County DHHS v. Julie A.B.
cases.holding: At the dispositional phase of a TPR the circuit court must treat the child's best interests as the prevailing factor, weighing the six Wis. Stat. sec. 48.426(3) factors and any others against that standard; applying a different standard (such as requiring 'egregious' unfitness) is an error of law.
cases.quote: The best interests of the child is the polestar for the court in a dispositional hearing, and a failure to apply that standard is an error of law.

relevance.DEC-03: It fixes what a substantiated finding can and cannot lead to: unfitness once grounds are proved, with best interests controlling only at the later dispositional stage.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the controlling Wisconsin statement of the disposition standard governing every TPR and adoption outcome.
relevance.OUT-05: It holds that a court may dismiss a TPR petition at disposition only if dismissal can be reconciled with the child's best interests, framing lawful case closure.

cases.holding: Wisconsin TPR proceeds in two phases: grounds/unfitness, which the petitioner must prove by clear and convincing evidence and where partial summary judgment is available when no material fact is disputed, followed by a dispositional phase governed by the child's best interests.
cases.quote: A finding of parental unfitness is a necessary prerequisite to termination of parental rights, but a finding of unfitness does not necessitate that parental rights be terminated.

relevance.DEC-03: It sets the evidentiary threshold - clear and convincing evidence of an enumerated ground - that an agency finding must ultimately support in court.
relevance.DEC-05: It defines the two-phase structure a county opens when it files a TPR petition and when summary disposition of the grounds phase is permissible.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the leading modern statement of Wisconsin's two-part TPR procedure and the gateway role of the unfitness finding.

cases.case_name: Kenosha County DHS v. Jodie W.
cases.holding: Terminating an incarcerated parent's rights under the continuing-CHIPS ground because she failed to meet a condition of return she could not possibly satisfy while imprisoned, without regard to her actual parenting or the child's condition, violates substantive due process.
cases.quote: the circuit court improperly deemed Jodie unfit solely by virtue of her status as an incarcerated person without regard for her actual parenting activities or the condition of her child

relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered conditions of return must be ones the particular parent can actually meet; impossible conditions cannot support later unfitness.
relevance.OUT-01: It constrains how a county may set and judge reunification conditions for a parent whose circumstances (here incarceration) limit compliance.
relevance.FAIL-05: It is Wisconsin's leading authority that treating a parent's status - incarceration - as a proxy for unfitness is unconstitutional.

cases.case_name: Monroe County DHS v. Kelli B.
cases.holding: The incestuous-parenthood ground for termination, applied to a mother who was herself the child victim of the incest, is not narrowly tailored to a compelling state interest and violates her substantive due process right to parent.
cases.quote: Because we determine that the statute, as applied, is not narrowly tailored to advance a compelling state interest, we conclude that it violates Kelli's right to substantive due process.

relevance.DEC-03: It shows that a statutory ground, even when factually established, must still survive strict scrutiny as applied to the particular parent.
relevance.FAIL-05: It is the Wisconsin precedent for challenging a termination ground that penalizes a parent for a status or circumstance rather than conduct.

cases.holding: The 'failure to assume parental responsibility' ground is measured by a totality-of-the-circumstances test looking at the parent's conduct across the child's entire life, and may include exposing the child to a hazardous living environment.
cases.quote: We conclude that a fact-finder should consider a parent's actions throughout the entirety of the child's life when determining whether he has assumed parental responsibility.

relevance.OUT-02: It supplies the governing test for one of the most frequently pleaded TPR grounds in Wisconsin.

cases.holding: A parent sanctioned with default for failing to appear personally in a TPR case retains the statutory right to counsel at both the fact-finding and dispositional phases, and the court may not find default before taking evidence that clearly and convincingly establishes grounds.
cases.quote: the circuit court erred in finding Shirley E. in default before conducting an evidentiary hearing to determine whether there was clear and convincing evidence that the grounds for termination existed

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the leading Wisconsin case vacating a termination order for denial of counsel and for defaulting a parent without proof of grounds.
relevance.OUT-02: It fixes the minimum procedure - counsel plus proof of grounds - that must precede any Wisconsin termination.

cases.case_name: Brown County DHS v. Brenda B.
cases.holding: A parent's no-contest plea to TPR grounds is knowing, voluntary and intelligent only if the colloquy informs the parent of the two dispositions available to the court; Brenda's colloquy was adequate and she made no prima facie showing otherwise.
cases.quote: To render a plea knowing, voluntary, and intelligent, we conclude that the parent must be informed of the two independent dispositions available to the circuit court.

relevance.FAIL-01: A defective plea colloquy is a recognized ground for reopening and reversing a Wisconsin termination order.
relevance.OUT-02: It states what a parent must be told before conceding grounds that lead to termination and adoption.

cases.case_name: Sheboygan County DHHS v. Tanya M.B.
cases.holding: A CHIPS dispositional order satisfies Wis. Stat. sec. 48.355(2)(b)1. without itemizing every service so long as it orders supervision, services and case management and sets detailed conditions; whether the agency made a 'reasonable effort' to provide those services is judged in light of the parents' cooperation.
cases.quote: A relevant consideration in determining "reasonable effort" to provide services is the parents' "level of cooperation."

relevance.ACT-01: It describes how voluntarily accepted services and parental cooperation are weighed when the agency's effort is later tested.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the controlling Wisconsin authority on what a court-ordered service plan must contain and how 'reasonable effort' is proved.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification turns on the same reasonable-effort showing this case defines.

cases.holding: The amendment to Wis. Stat. sec. 48.23(3) barring courts from appointing counsel for anyone but the child in CHIPS cases violates the separation of powers and the Due Process Clause; courts must retain discretion to appoint counsel for parents case by case.
cases.quote: We conclude that fundamental fairness requires that a circuit judge be given the discretion to make the determination of what due process requires on a case-by-case basis.

relevance.DEC-05: When a county files a CHIPS petition, the circuit court retains discretion to appoint counsel for an indigent parent.
relevance.INP-04: It governs a judge's authority over counsel and process once a child-protection matter is before the court.

cases.holding: Wisconsin's Children's Code requires that a parent who appears in a termination proceeding actually be represented by counsel in court; absent a knowing and voluntary waiver established by careful questioning, the resulting order cannot stand.
cases.quote: it becomes the duty of the court to determine by careful questioning that the waiver of counsel's presence is knowledgeable and voluntary

relevance.DEC-05: It sets the representation prerequisite that attaches as soon as a petition brings a parent before the juvenile court.
relevance.INP-04: It defines the court's own duty toward an unrepresented parent at the first hearing in a Children's Code case.

cases.case_name: Sallie T. v. Milwaukee County DHHS
cases.holding: A biological parent's compliance with the return-home conditions of a CHIPS dispositional order creates no presumption that returning the child is in the child's best interests; revision or extension remains a discretionary best-interests decision.
cases.quote: We determine that compliance with a dispositional order is not dispositive of a child's best interests.

relevance.INP-05: A parent's own request to have a child returned is judged on best interests, not on checklist compliance.
relevance.ACT-01: Completing voluntary or ordered services does not by itself entitle a family to closure or return.
relevance.ACT-02: It defines the legal weight of compliance with a court-ordered service plan.
relevance.DEC-06: It supports engaging families with services while keeping the best-interests judgment with the court.
relevance.OUT-01: It is the controlling Wisconsin authority on when reunification is warranted after conditions are met.

cases.holding: Wis. Stat. sec. 48.424(4), which requires a finding of unfitness once statutory grounds are proved, comports with substantive due process because the court retains discretion at disposition to dismiss the petition if termination is not warranted.
cases.quote: The discretion that the statute vests in the court to dismiss the petition for termination if it finds termination is not warranted under the standards assures full, substantive due process.

relevance.DEC-03: It explains why a proven statutory ground compels an unfitness finding without offending due process.
relevance.OUT-05: It preserves the circuit court's power to dismiss a termination petition outright at disposition.

cases.holding: A juvenile court loses competency to act when a CHIPS dispositional order expires without a timely extension hearing beyond the single 30-day continuance, and no party can waive that loss of competency.
cases.quote: we hold that a party cannot waive the right to object to a court's loss of competence once the 30-day extension has passed without a hearing

relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered supervision ends by operation of law if the extension deadline passes, regardless of the parties' acquiescence.
relevance.OUT-01: It marks when agency authority over a family lapses and the child must be returned.
relevance.OUT-04: It governs the expiration and extension of the dispositional orders that keep a youth in out-of-home care.
relevance.OUT-05: Loss of competency is a mandatory, non-waivable basis for ending a CHIPS case.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the Wisconsin Supreme Court's core authority for vacating juvenile orders entered after the court lost competency.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of James D.K.
cases.holding: Over a parent's objection a court may appoint a nonparent guardian of a minor only on a showing of extraordinary circumstances affecting the child's health or safety, and then only if the appointment is in the child's best interests.
cases.quote: a court is authorized under chapter 880 to appoint a nonparent as guardian of a minor if there exist extraordinary circumstances affecting the health or safety of the minor

relevance.INP-05: It is the standard applied when a relative or caregiver asks a court to take responsibility for a child without a CPS petition.
relevance.ACT-04: It sets the threshold a kin caregiver must meet to obtain legal authority over a child when a parent objects.
relevance.ACT-06: Extraordinary circumstances requiring medical aid are an express basis for appointing a guardian to authorize care.
relevance.OUT-03: It is the controlling Wisconsin standard for nonparent guardianship as a permanency outcome.

cases.holding: A social worker and police officer may enter a home without a warrant to check on children reported abused only if the officer is actually motivated by a need to render aid and, objectively, a reasonable person would have believed an emergency existed.
cases.quote: Both tests must be satisfied before a warrantless entry will be justified under the emergency rule exception.

relevance.INP-02: It tests when an unverified third-party report is enough to justify entering a home without a warrant.
relevance.INP-03: It is the Wisconsin standard for a joint police and social-worker response to an abuse report.
relevance.INP-06: An anonymous or unnamed caller's tip supports entry only if its basis of knowledge and reliability create an objective belief in an emergency.
relevance.INP-10: It marks the constitutional line an intake screen must clear before workers enter a family's home.
relevance.INP-12: It supplies the exigency test that legitimizes taking a child into protective custody without prior judicial authorization.
relevance.DEC-02: Accepting a report for investigation does not by itself authorize a warrantless entry; the two-part emergency test must be met.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the Wisconsin exigency standard against which an emergency removal decision is judged.
relevance.ACT-06: It authorizes immediate entry where children are believed to need aid for actual or threatened physical injury.

cases.holding: The strict-liability prohibition in Wis. Stat. sec. 48.981(7) on disclosing child-abuse report information reaches only communications of information the recipient did not already know.
cases.quote: we hold, for the purposes of § 48.981(7), that "disclose" is defined to require that the information communicated must have been previously unknown by the recipient

relevance.INP-01: It defines the confidentiality duty that attaches to a mandated reporter's report and to those who receive it.
relevance.INP-02: It governs the secrecy of a third-party report and the identity of the reporter.
relevance.INP-06: It is the authority protecting hotline reporters' identities and report contents from disclosure.
relevance.INP-07: Medical and other professional reporters are protected by the same confidentiality rule construed here.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated finding carries statutory confidentiality restrictions on the underlying report record.
relevance.FAIL-06: It marks the boundary between unlawful disclosure and lawful communication of child-protection records.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the criminal backstop that limits what child-abuse report information can be released to the public.

cases.holding: Foster children have a clearly established Fourteenth Amendment right to safe and secure placement; the conduct of the officials who place and supervise them is measured by the professional judgment standard, and those officials were not entitled to qualified immunity.
cases.quote: Accordingly, we conclude that the duty of public officials to provide foster children with a safe and secure placement is based on a professional judgment standard.

relevance.ACT-03: It is the Wisconsin Supreme Court's statement of the constitutional duty owed to a child the state places in foster care.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the controlling Wisconsin authority for damages when a child is seriously harmed while in agency placement.
relevance.FAIL-03: It converts placement and supervision failures into an enforceable constitutional duty rather than mere program non-compliance.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the route to liability when a child is abused or killed in a placement the county selected and supervised.
relevance.PMC-01: It gives a judicially enforceable content to the safety outcomes the federal CFSR measures.
relevance.PMC-06: It identifies placement safety as the systemic weak point Wisconsin courts will actually police.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Angela M.W. v. Kruzicki
cases.holding: The definition of 'child' in Wis. Stat. sec. 48.02(2) does not include a viable fetus, so the juvenile court had no Children's Code jurisdiction to take a pregnant woman into custody to protect her fetus.
cases.quote: we hold that the definition of "child" in § 48.02(2) does not include a viable fetus

relevance.INP-07: It limits the reach of a prenatal medical disclosure: a report about a fetus did not then trigger Children's Code jurisdiction.
relevance.INP-12: It marks the outer jurisdictional limit of protective custody under ch. 48.
relevance.ACT-05: It holds that a protective order confining a person cannot rest on Children's Code authority absent a 'child' within the statute.

cases.case_name: Eau Claire County DHS v. S.E.
cases.holding: TPR warning notice under Wis. Stat. sec. 48.356 must identify the grounds, including sub-parts, applicable when the CHIPS order is entered; a later amendment shortening the continuing-CHIPS timeframe did not require new notice and did not violate due process.
cases.quote: Sophie's notice needed to identify only the grounds for termination that existed at the time of the initial CHIPS order.

relevance.ACT-02: Every court order continuing out-of-home placement must carry written warning of the TPR grounds then applicable.
relevance.DEC-05: Valid warning notice at the CHIPS stage is a statutory prerequisite to a later TPR petition.

cases.holding: Deciding a contested TPR issue in the State's favor before the parent has had the opportunity to present a case-in-chief is structural error requiring automatic reversal and a new trial.
cases.quote: We hold that denying a defendant the opportunity to present his case-in-chief is a structural error, the consequence of which is an automatic new trial.

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the strongest recent Wisconsin ground for reversing a termination outright, without harmless-error analysis.

cases.holding: Wisconsin's public records law applies to a completed police investigative report and creates a strong presumption in favor of release; here the subject's privacy and reputational interests did not overcome that presumption.
cases.quote: We hold that the open records law applies to the Report in this case and there is thus a strong presumption in favor of release.

relevance.INP-09: It is the mechanism by which outside reviewers actually obtain the investigative records that trigger oversight.
relevance.FAIL-06: It establishes that withholding a completed government report requires a specific, record-based justification.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and oversight records held by Wisconsin agencies are presumptively open under the rule stated here.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review bodies rely on this presumption of openness to obtain agency material.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the controlling Wisconsin open-records balancing test for transparency requests.
relevance.PMC-06: Any systemic analysis of Wisconsin child welfare depends on the presumption of release this case enforces.

cases.case_name: Monroe County DHS v. Luis R.
cases.holding: ICWA sec. 1912(f) applies in a TPR even though the Indian child was already placed outside the parental home, and a county social worker without expertise beyond ordinary social-work qualifications is not a 'qualified expert witness'; sec. 1912(d) carries no beyond-a-reasonable-doubt burden.
cases.quote: We conclude that 25 U.S.C. § 1912 (f) applies even though the child has been placed outside the parental home before the TPR proceeding is filed.

relevance.INP-11: It is Wisconsin's leading published decision on how ICWA attaches once a case involves an Indian child.
relevance.ACT-04: ICWA's remedial-services and expert-witness requirements shape placement decisions for Indian children.
relevance.FAIL-05: Failure to apply ICWA's protections to an Indian family is a reversible, rights-based failure in Wisconsin.

cases.holding: In a TPR involving an Indian child the trial court correctly imposed a dual burden: proof beyond a reasonable doubt of ICWA's active-efforts and serious-damage elements, alongside the Children's Code elements.
cases.quote: We conclude that the trial court appropriately distributed the burden of proof according to the dictates of both the ICWA and the Wisconsin children's code.

relevance.INP-11: It establishes that ICWA supersedes the Children's Code in any covered custody proceeding in Wisconsin.
relevance.ACT-04: It requires proof of active efforts to prevent the breakup of the Indian family before an Indian child's ties are severed.

cases.holding: Before denying a parent's ICWA request to transfer a case to tribal court, the circuit court must first ascertain whether the tribal court will accept jurisdiction and then decide whether good cause exists to deny transfer.
cases.quote: We conclude that reversal is appropriate and, on remand, direct the circuit court to first ascertain whether the tribal court will accept jurisdiction.

relevance.INP-11: It is the Wisconsin procedure for an ICWA transfer-to-tribal-court request.
relevance.ACT-04: Tribal jurisdiction, once accepted, governs placement decisions for an Indian child.
relevance.OUT-03: Transfer to tribal court can redirect the entire permanency path, including tribal customary guardianship.

cases.holding: A prior JIPS disposition as to the children does not preclude the county from obtaining a CHIPS disposition against the parents on the same facts; JIPS and CHIPS are distinct proceedings with different parties and purposes.
cases.quote: a JIPS disposition and a CHIPS disposition are two distinct areas of law, and a disposition in the JIPS case did not preclude a disposition in the CHIPS cases

relevance.INP-04: A juvenile-justice referral does not exhaust the court's ability to order child-protection proceedings against the parents.
relevance.DEC-05: It confirms a county may file CHIPS petitions even after a related juvenile disposition has been entered.
relevance.OUT-04: It distinguishes the juvenile-justice and child-welfare tracks that determine which orders continue as a youth ages.

cases.holding: Wis. Stat. sec. 48.981(4) immunity extends to persons who in good faith relay suspected abuse information to someone expected to report it, not only to the individual who contacts authorities; good faith is presumed and conclusory allegations do not rebut it.
cases.quote: Because we conclude that the trial court properly determined that the respondents were statutorily immune from liability, the judgment is affirmed.

relevance.INP-01: It is the Wisconsin construction of the mandated-reporter immunity a reporter relies on.
relevance.INP-02: Non-mandated third parties who report in good faith receive the same statutory immunity.
relevance.INP-06: It confirms the presumption of good faith that protects hotline and informal reporters from suit.
relevance.INP-07: Health professionals who pass information to a designated reporter remain within the immunity.
relevance.INP-08: It squarely addresses school personnel who report through a designated staff member rather than directly.

cases.holding: Wisconsin recognizes no damages claim against caseworkers for intentional interference with 'family unity,' and in any event county social workers are immune for discretionary acts; conclusory allegations of malice do not pierce that immunity.
cases.quote: public officers and employees enjoy immunity from suit for discretionary actions undertaken in the scope of their public employment

relevance.INP-10: Decisions to escalate or not escalate an intake are discretionary acts shielded from damages suits.
relevance.DEC-01: A screen-out or closure decision is discretionary and not actionable in tort absent a ministerial duty.
relevance.DEC-02: How an accepted case is investigated is a discretionary judgment protected by immunity.
relevance.DEC-06: Choosing services over a petition is a discretionary path the courts will not second-guess in damages.
relevance.ACT-01: A caseworker's choices about which services to offer a family are discretionary and immune.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the principal Wisconsin obstacle to a state-law damages claim arising from a wrongful child-welfare intervention.
relevance.PMC-02: It shows that accountability for caseworker conduct in Wisconsin runs through oversight and audit rather than tort.

cases.holding: A caseworker's change of a child's placement without the notice required by Wis. Stat. sec. 48.357(1) was random and unauthorized conduct for which adequate state postdeprivation remedies exist, defeating a federal procedural due process claim; no special relationship created a substantive due process duty.
cases.quote: the trial court properly dismissed the procedural due process claim because Chorlton's actions were random and unauthorized, and adequate postdeprivation state law remedies exist

relevance.DEC-01: Where the state did not create the danger, its failure to act does not create federal due process liability.
relevance.ACT-03: It addresses the notice owed before a county changes a child's placement and the remedy when notice is skipped.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the Wisconsin application of DeShaney to serious injuries following an agency placement decision.
relevance.FAIL-02: It defines when a statutory placement violation does - and does not - become a federal constitutional claim.
relevance.FAIL-04: It shows the narrow path to liability when harm follows a county's unauthorized placement decision.

cases.holding: A juvenile court may order disclosure of otherwise confidential agency records under Wis. Stat. sec. 48.78(2)(a) as a reasonable exercise of its discretion, and that order was lawful here.
cases.quote: the juvenile court order for disclosure was a reasonable exercise of lawful authority under § 48.78(2)(a), STATS.

relevance.INP-04: It is the authority for a judge to order agency records opened in the course of a child-protection matter.
relevance.INP-09: Oversight bodies and the press obtain juvenile agency records only through the judicial route described here.
relevance.FAIL-06: It supplies the lawful mechanism for compelled disclosure when an agency refuses to release records.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review of agency conduct depends on the court-ordered disclosure power recognized here.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality and serious-incident review requires exactly the sec. 48.78(2)(a) disclosure this case upholds.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the confidentiality exception that makes transparency in Wisconsin juvenile records possible.

cases.holding: The 30-day time limits in Wis. Stat. secs. 48.30(6) and 48.31(7) are mandatory; failure to meet them deprives the juvenile court of competency to hear the petition, requiring the dispositional orders to be vacated and the petitions dismissed.
cases.quote: We conclude that the thirty-day time limit in each section is mandatory.

relevance.DEC-05: Filing a CHIPS petition starts mandatory clocks that, if missed, cost the court its competency.
relevance.OUT-04: Continued juvenile-court authority over a youth depends on meeting these mandatory deadlines.
relevance.OUT-05: Missing the statutory deadlines compels dismissal of the petition.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the classic Wisconsin basis for vacating juvenile orders entered outside the statutory time limits.

cases.holding: The shortened notice-of-appeal deadline for TPR cases does not interfere with effective assistance of appellate counsel, is supported by a rational basis, and does not offend the separation of powers.
cases.quote: the fifteen-day time limit does not interfere with effective assistance of appellate counsel

relevance.FAIL-01: It governs the compressed appellate timeline a parent must meet to challenge a termination order.

cases.case_name: Estate of Hammersley v. Wisconsin County Mutual Insurance Co.
cases.holding: A county crisis worker who investigated a report and declined an emergency detention acted in good faith as a matter of law and is immune under Wis. Stat. sec. 51.15(11) from liability for the killings that followed.
cases.quote: In light of these undisputed facts, we conclude that no reasonable fact-finder could infer a lack of good faith.

relevance.ACT-06: It is the Wisconsin standard governing a county worker's decision whether to compel emergency psychiatric care.
relevance.OUT-06: It shows how Wisconsin courts treat civil claims arising from a death that follows a county's emergency-response decision.
relevance.FAIL-04: Good-faith statutory immunity is the principal defense when a child dies after an agency declined to intervene.
relevance.PMC-04: It illustrates why fatality review, not litigation, is the practical accountability mechanism in Wisconsin.

cases.holding: Wisconsin had initial child-custody jurisdiction under the UCCJEA and the circuit court properly exercised its discretion in awarding guardianship of the child to her maternal grandmother and step-grandfather on compelling reasons.
cases.quote: Here, we conclude that the circuit court properly exercised its discretion in awarding guardianship of Alexis to Stephen and Ilya.

relevance.INP-05: It is the path a relative uses to seek legal responsibility for a child without a CPS petition.
relevance.ACT-04: It shows how Wisconsin courts place a child with kin over a parent's objection.
relevance.OUT-03: It is a worked example of kinship guardianship as a permanency outcome, including the jurisdictional predicate.

cases.holding: Grounds for a child abuse injunction under Wis. Stat. sec. 813.122 must be established on pre-petition evidence; post-filing treatment or remedial steps bear only on the type and extent of visitation if the injunction issues.
cases.quote: for the purpose of determining whether grounds exist to issue a child abuse injunction pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 813.122 , a trial court may consider only pre-petition evidence

relevance.ACT-05: It is the controlling Wisconsin rule on what evidence supports a child abuse restraining order and injunction.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: Wisconsin caseworkers violated the Fourth Amendment and the plaintiffs' right to familial relations by entering a private school and seizing and interviewing a child without a warrant, court order, probable cause, exigent circumstances, or parental or school consent.
cases.quote: Thus, although child welfare caseworkers may investigate allegations of child abuse without violating parents' constitutional right to familial relations, they may not do so arbitrarily.

relevance.INP-01: It holds that a report from a mandated reporter does not by itself authorize a warrantless custodial interview of a child.
relevance.INP-03: It governs how Wisconsin caseworkers and officers may act on a referral about corporal punishment.
relevance.INP-08: It is the leading Seventh Circuit case on interviewing a child at school without parental consent - and it arose in Wisconsin.
relevance.INP-10: Escalating a screened report to an on-site child interview is itself a Fourth Amendment seizure requiring justification.
relevance.DEC-02: It sets the constitutional limits on how an accepted Wisconsin investigation may be conducted.
relevance.DEC-04: Even a threat to remove children, without reasonable suspicion of parental abuse, violates the right to familial relations.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the controlling circuit authority for unlawful seizure and investigation claims arising in Wisconsin.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: A Racine County caseworker who removed a child on neglect allegations was entitled to qualified immunity because a reasonable caseworker could have believed probable cause existed, and no evidence showed that probable cause dissipated before the court's probable-cause order two days later.
cases.quote: However, the continued withholding of a minor may constitute a constitutional violation where probable cause or reasonable suspicion dissipates.

relevance.INP-03: It arises from a joint law-enforcement and county response to a report of a child left home alone in Wisconsin.
relevance.INP-12: It confirms that taking a child into protective custody is a Fourth Amendment seizure needing court order, probable cause, or exigency.
relevance.ACT-03: Continued foster placement must remain supported by probable cause or it becomes an ongoing seizure.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the Seventh Circuit's Wisconsin-based application of the probable-cause standard to an emergency removal decision.
relevance.FAIL-02: It defines both the claim and the qualified-immunity defense for a wrongful removal suit in Wisconsin.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: A child removed from his home on knowingly false allegations of neglect, without investigation, a pre-deprivation hearing, or exigent circumstances, states Fourth Amendment, substantive and procedural due process claims under sec. 1983 against the officials involved.
cases.quote: at a minimum it requires that government officials not misrepresent the facts in order to obtain the removal of a child from his parents

relevance.INP-12: It holds that taking a child into custody for questioning, without parental consent, is a seizure.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the Seventh Circuit's baseline: removal is reasonable only on a court order, probable cause, or exigency.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the leading circuit authority that a removal procured by misrepresentation is actionable under sec. 1983.

cases.case_name: K.H. ex rel. Murphy v. Morgan
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: Once the state removes a child and assumes custody, officials may not deliberately and without justification place the child with caregivers known to be likely to abuse or neglect her; doing so violates substantive due process.
cases.quote: Once the state assumes custody of a person, it owes him a rudimentary duty of safekeeping no matter how perilous his circumstances when he was free.

relevance.ACT-03: It is the circuit-level source of the constitutional duty owed to a child the state places in foster care.
relevance.FAIL-04: It supplies the deliberate-placement-in-danger theory available when a child is harmed in state-arranged care.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative obligation on a county social services agency to protect a child from violence by his father where the child is not in state custody, even though the agency knew of the danger and failed to act.
cases.quote: As a general matter, then, we conclude that a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause.

relevance.DEC-01: It is the constitutional consequence of screening out or closing a report: generally no federal liability for failing to intervene.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the governing federal rule - decided on Wisconsin facts - when a child is killed or maimed after agency inaction.
relevance.FAIL-03: Federal performance failures are enforced through funding and oversight, not through a constitutional damages action.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the threshold barrier in every Wisconsin child-death case where the child remained at home.
relevance.PMC-01: It explains why CFSR monitoring, not litigation, is the operative accountability mechanism for safety failures.
relevance.PMC-04: It arose from Winnebago County, Wisconsin, and is the case that drove modern fatality-review reform.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Due process requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child.
cases.quote: The fundamental liberty interest of natural parents in the care, custody, and management of their child does not evaporate simply because they have not been model parents

relevance.DEC-03: It is the federal floor: an agency finding cannot support severance of parental rights on anything less than clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the constitutional standard of proof underlying Wisconsin's TPR grounds phase.

cases.holding: In a custody dispute between a parent and a third party the best-interests test does not govern; a parent is entitled to custody unless the parent is unfit or unable to care for the child or compelling reasons exist, and only then may the court award custody to a third party on best interests.
cases.quote: Compelling reasons include abandonment, persistent neglect of parental responsibilities, extended disruption of parental custody, or other similar extraordinary circumstances that would drastically affect the welfare of the child.

relevance.INP-05: It is the source rule a relative or caregiver must satisfy when asking a court for responsibility for a child over a parent's objection, without any CPS petition.
relevance.ACT-04: It defines the 'compelling reasons' and 'extraordinary circumstances' threshold that every Wisconsin kinship-placement fight between a parent and kin is measured against.
relevance.OUT-03: It is the foundational Wisconsin standard that James D.K. and Stephen R. apply when guardianship or third-party custody is the permanency outcome.

cases.case_name: Evelyn C. R. v. Tykila S.
cases.holding: A circuit court may sanction a parent who violates an order to appear personally by entering default, but it erroneously exercises its discretion if it enters default on the grounds phase without first taking evidence sufficient to establish the ground by clear and convincing evidence; here the error was harmless because the dispositional testimony supplied that proof.
cases.quote: By entering a default judgment against Tykila on the issue of abandonment without first taking this constitutionally and statutorily required evidence, the circuit court erroneously exercised its discretion.

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the controlling Wisconsin authority a practitioner reaches for first when attacking a TPR default entered without proof of grounds - the decision Shirley E. later builds on.
relevance.DEC-05: It defines what the circuit court must actually do once a TPR petition is filed and a parent fails to appear: take evidence before any finding of unfitness.

cases.holding: The Wisconsin legislature intended the statutory right to appointed counsel in a termination of parental rights proceeding to include the right to effective counsel, so the court did not reach the parents' constitutional arguments and remanded for a Machner hearing on trial counsel's performance.
cases.quote: It is axiomatic that the right to be represented by appointed counsel is worthless unless that right includes the right to effective counsel.

relevance.DEC-05: It completes the representation guarantee that attaches when a petition brings an indigent parent before the juvenile court: appointment alone is not enough, the lawyer must be effective.
relevance.FAIL-01: Ineffective assistance of appointed trial counsel is an independent Wisconsin ground for setting aside a termination order, and this is the case that establishes it.

cases.case_name: Dane County Department of Human Services v. Ponn P.
cases.holding: The continuing-denial-of-placement ground in Wis. Stat. sec. 48.415(4) is narrowly tailored and does not violate substantive due process on its face, because the required unfitness finding rests on the cumulative effect of the earlier judicial determinations that must precede it; a parent who pled no contest and never contested the underlying order could not mount an as-applied challenge.
cases.quote: It is the cumulative effect of the determinations made at each of the previous steps that causes the finding made under § 48.415(4) to amount to unfitness.

relevance.OUT-02: It is the immediate predecessor to Brenda B. and the Wisconsin Supreme Court's statement of what a no-contest plea to TPR grounds concedes and forfeits.
relevance.FAIL-01: It marks the line between a preserved as-applied constitutional challenge and one forfeited by pleading no contest, which determines whether a termination can be undone on appeal.

cases.holding: Only the last order placing a child outside the home before a TPR petition is filed must carry the written sec. 48.356(2) warning, and although the circuit court erred under sec. 48.422(3) by failing to hear testimony supporting the petition's allegations, Steven H. was not prejudiced.
cases.quote: We conclude that the legislature intended the circuit court to hear testimony in support of the allegations because testimony safeguards accurate fact-finding and protects the parents.

relevance.DEC-05: It fixes which out-of-home placement orders must carry the TPR warning before a county may file a petition, and what the court must hear once it does.
relevance.OUT-02: It states the evidentiary step - testimony supporting the petition's allegations - that must precede any Wisconsin termination even when the parent does not contest grounds.

cases.case_name: State v. Bobby G. (In re Marquette S.)
cases.holding: In deciding whether a biological father failed to assume parental responsibility under Wis. Stat. sec. 48.415(6), the circuit court must consider the efforts he made after learning he is the father and before the grounds are adjudicated; the contrary partial summary judgment was reversed and the cause remanded for fact-finding.
cases.quote: a circuit court must consider the biological father's efforts undertaken after he discovers that he is the father but before the circuit court adjudicates the grounds of the termination proceeding

relevance.DEC-03: It limits what evidence a proven ground may rest on: a father's post-notice efforts count at the grounds phase, so an agency's early record cannot alone fix unfitness.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the companion to Tammy W-G. on the failure-to-assume ground and controls when summary judgment on that ground is available before termination.

cases.case_name: Hernandez ex rel. Hernandez v. Foster
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: A child's initial removal supported by probable cause is reasonable, but continuing to hold the child in protective custody after probable cause and reasonable suspicion have dissipated states Fourth Amendment and substantive due process claims that survive qualified immunity.
cases.quote: Nor does it suggest that the state may retain custody of a child for up to forty-eight hours where probable cause and even reasonable suspicion no longer exist.

relevance.INP-12: It is the Seventh Circuit's fullest statement that protective custody is a continuing seizure that must remain justified for as long as it lasts.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the case Xiong applies, and the anchor authority on what a caseworker must know before removing a child and how long that justification lasts.
relevance.FAIL-02: It supplies the removal and continued-withholding claims, and the coerced-safety-plan claim, that a Wisconsin family can bring under sec. 1983 in this circuit.

cases.case_name: Siliven v. Indiana Department of Child Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: Caseworkers who removed a two-year-old without a court order had probable cause to believe he would be seriously endangered if not immediately removed, the scope of the removal was limited to that exigency, and they were therefore entitled to qualified immunity.
cases.quote: The pertinent inquiry, then, is whether defendants had probable cause to believe that C.S.'s physical health would be seriously endangered if he was not immediately removed from his father's custody.

relevance.DEC-04: It states the exact question a Wisconsin county must be able to answer before removing a child without a court order, and how narrowly the removal must then be tailored.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: A caseworker's visual examination of a child's body during a child-abuse investigation is a search within the Fourth Amendment, but neither a warrant nor probable cause is required; its constitutionality turns on contextual reasonableness, which this preliminary record could not resolve, so the denial of an injunction and the individual defendants' qualified immunity were affirmed.
cases.quote: Therefore, whether a search is "reasonable," in the constitutional sense, will vary according to the context of the search.

relevance.INP-08: It is the foundational circuit framework for a CPS bodily examination of a child conducted away from home, including at school.
relevance.INP-10: Escalating a hotline report to an on-site examination of a child is a search whose reasonableness must be justified by more than the screening criteria themselves.
relevance.DEC-02: It is the reasonableness-balancing framework Doe v. Heck expressly applies to how an accepted investigation may intrude on a child.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: A Bureau of Milwaukee Child Welfare caseworker who conducted under-the-clothes examinations of two children at their private school without a warrant, probable cause, parental consent or exigent circumstances violated clearly established Fourth Amendment rights, and Wis. Stat. sec. 48.981(3)(c)1. did not make her conduct reasonable.
cases.quote: it is a violation of a child's constitutional rights to conduct a search of a child at a private school without a warrant or probable cause, consent, or exigent circumstances

relevance.INP-08: It is the single most useful authority for a Wisconsin school-based CPS contact, holding that a general principal's consent does not authorize searching a child.
relevance.DEC-02: It confirms that a Wisconsin agency policy permitting on-site child contact cannot override the Fourth Amendment limits on how an investigation is conducted.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the Wisconsin follow-on to Doe v. Heck in which qualified immunity was denied, making it the clearest path to caseworker liability in this circuit.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: Disclosure of an administrative 'indicated' child-abuse finding to employers deprives child care workers and career entrants of a protected liberty interest, entitling them to pre-indication notice and an opportunity to respond plus prompt post-deprivation review, while the agency may retain a 'credible evidence' standard that requires weighing exculpatory as well as inculpatory evidence; foster parents have no comparable career or property interest.
cases.quote: we believe that the imposition of this added legal impediment constitutes a very tangible loss of employment opportunities due to the disclosure of the indicated report

relevance.DEC-03: It is the controlling circuit authority on the due process owed before an agency records a substantiated finding and puts it on a central register - the node Wisconsin case law leaves empty.
relevance.DEC-02: It requires an investigator to weigh evidence that the incident did not occur, not merely to find some evidence that it did, which is the federal floor for Wisconsin investigative practice.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that a state make 'reasonable efforts' to prevent removal and to reunify families confers no privately enforceable right on children or families and creates no implied cause of action.
cases.quote: We conclude that 42 U. S. C. § 671 (a)(15) neither confers an enforceable private right on its beneficiaries nor creates an implied cause of action on their behalf.

relevance.FAIL-03: It is the dispositive holding - not an inference - that federal child-welfare performance requirements are enforced through funding and oversight rather than private damages or injunction suits.
relevance.ACT-02: The federal reasonable-efforts requirement behind Wisconsin's court-ordered service plans cannot itself be enforced by the family in federal court.
relevance.PMC-01: It explains why CFSR review and the Secretary's funding leverage, not litigation, are the operative accountability mechanism for federal performance standards.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: ICWA sec. 1912(f)'s heightened showing does not apply where the parent never had legal or physical custody of the Indian child, and sec. 1912(d)'s remedial-and-rehabilitative-efforts requirement applies only where terminating the parent's rights would precipitate the breakup of an Indian family.
cases.quote: we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights.

relevance.INP-11: It limits when ICWA's heightened protections attach once a case involves an Indian child, and it postdates and narrows Wisconsin's Luis R. line.
relevance.ACT-04: It confines the active/remedial efforts obligation that otherwise shapes placement decisions for an Indian child to cases where an existing Indian family would be broken up.
relevance.FAIL-05: Any claim that ICWA's protections were denied to an Indian family must now be framed within the custody and family-breakup limits this decision imposes.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court rejected every challenge to the Indian Child Welfare Act - upholding Congress's Article I authority to enact it, rejecting the anticommandeering claims on the merits, and finding no standing for the equal protection and nondelegation claims - leaving ICWA's placement preferences and procedural requirements intact.
cases.quote: we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing.

relevance.INP-11: It confirms that ICWA remains binding on Wisconsin counties and state courts, so the tribal-jurisdiction and notice machinery in the Wisconsin ICWA line is current law.
relevance.ACT-04: It leaves ICWA's placement preferences for Indian children in force against equal-protection and anticommandeering attack, which is the predicate for every kinship and tribal placement decision.

notes: Wisconsin's child-welfare case law is statutory and concentrated in ch. 48 (Children's Code) TPR and CHIPS appeals; the Wisconsin Supreme Court has produced a dense body of law on termination of parental rights but very little on the front end of CPS practice (screening, differential response, substantiated-finding appeals).

No published Wisconsin decision was found reviewing an administrative 'substantiated' finding or a central-registry/caregiver-misconduct listing on due-process grounds. That gap is now filled at DEC-03 by Seventh Circuit law binding on Wisconsin counties (Dupuy v. Samuels), rather than by the TPR burden-of-proof cases alone.

No published Wisconsin decision was found on Differential Response / Alternative Response as such (DEC-06), on voluntary safety plans as a distinct legal device (ACT-01), or on extended foster care / the Chafee program and jurisdiction past age 18 (OUT-04). Those nodes are covered by the closest Wisconsin authority on dispositional-order duration, competency and CHIPS/JIPS jurisdiction (Green County v. H.N., T.H. v. La Crosse County, W.A.B. v. W.G.B.), and by Sallie T. on the legal weight of compliance with a service plan.

No published Wisconsin decision was found on race, religion, sex or disability discrimination in placement or investigation (FAIL-05, MEPA/Title VI). FAIL-05 is carried by the Wisconsin cases that invalidate status-based termination (Jodie W., Kelli B.), by the ICWA line (Luis R.), and now by Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, which sets the current federal limits on that one placement-equality regime Wisconsin courts actively enforce.

No Wisconsin case law was found on CFSR monitoring, OIG/Single Audit findings, Citizen Review Panels, the Protect Our Kids Act commission, or children who go missing from care. The PMC-family nodes and INP-09 are therefore served by the Wisconsin public-records and juvenile-records-disclosure line (Linzmeyer v. Forcey, In re Peter B., State v. Polashek) plus DeShaney, Kara B. and now Suter v. Artist M., which together mark the boundary between judicially enforceable duties and duties enforced only through federal funding and monitoring. This is a genuine gap, not an omission.

Every case in this brief was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its opinion text read. All quotes are exact substrings of the majority (or lead) opinion after whitespace and quote-mark normalization; no syllabus, headnote, dissent or concurrence text was used. For each of the fourteen cases added in this pass the quote was programmatically verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text and confirmed by paragraph position to fall inside the opinion of the court (for Ponn P. the majority ends at para. 35, before the Prosser concurrence; for Adoptive Couple and Brackeen the quotes sit inside the 'Opinion of the Court' sections; for Suter the quote is the final sentence of the majority, immediately preceding Justice Blackmun's dissent).
No unpublished or per curiam memorandum decisions were used. All 52 cases are published.

Practice warning: Sheboygan County DHHS v. Julie A.B., 2002 WI 95, expressly modified B.L.J. v. Polk County DSS and overruled In re Kelly S. on the disposition standard. B.L.J. is cited here only for the due-process rationale for the mandatory unfitness finding (sec. 48.424(4)), which Julie A.B. left intact; do not cite B.L.J.'s 'egregious unfitness' language.

Practice warning: Steven V. v. Kelley H., 2004 WI 47, withdrew the language of In re Elizabeth W. that had barred summary judgment in TPR proceedings. Summary judgment remains unavailable at the dispositional phase.

Practice warning: Monroe County DHS v. Luis R., 2009 WI App 109, construed ICWA sec. 1912(f) before Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl (2013) and before Wisconsin enacted its own Indian Child Welfare Act (WICWA, Wis. Stat. sec. 48.028, 2009 Wis. Act 94). Adoptive Couple is now included and must be read with Luis R. No published Wisconsin appellate decision construing WICWA's active-efforts or qualified-expert-witness provisions was located in CourtListener; practitioners should shepardize and check WICWA text directly.

The cluster records for Steven V. v. Kelley H. (2004 WI 47), Eau Claire County DHS v. S.E. (2021 WI 56) and Dane County DHS v. Ponn P. (2005 WI 32) carry only the Wisconsin public-domain citation and, for Ponn P., the Wis. 2d citation; the parallel N.W.2d citations are not in those clusters and were therefore not asserted here even where the opinion text displays them.

DeShaney v. Winnebago County DSS, Doe v. Heck and Michael C. v. Gresbach all arose out of Wisconsin agencies, so the federal authorities in this brief are not merely persuasive background - they are the governing law for Wisconsin counties in the Seventh Circuit. Hernandez (Illinois), Siliven (Indiana), Darryl H. (Illinois), Dupuy (Illinois) and Brokaw (Illinois) are Seventh Circuit decisions and bind Wisconsin counties equally, though their facts arose elsewhere.

The layers.case_law.key_cases entries already in the WI node files (e.g. 'Dane County DHS v. J. K.', 'Jane Doe v. Jay C. Lick, D.O.', 'Waushara County DHS v. A. M. S.') are keyword-matched recent listings with synthetic citations. None of them survived retrieval and review as on-point authority for these nodes and none is carried forward here.

Added Barstad v. Frazier (118 Wis. 2d 549) for INP-05, ACT-04 and OUT-03: it is the foundational Wisconsin Supreme Court rule for parent-versus-third-party custody and guardianship disputes, and both James D.K. and Stephen R. are applications of it; the brief previously cited the derivatives without the source.

Added Evelyn C. R. v. Tykila S. (2001 WI 110) for FAIL-01 and DEC-05: it is the controlling Wisconsin authority that a TPR default may not be entered on the grounds phase without evidence sufficient to prove the ground by clear and convincing evidence - the decision Shirley E. later builds on - and it also shows that the error can be cured by adequate dispositional testimony.

Added In Interest of M.D.(S) (168 Wis. 2d 995) for DEC-05 and FAIL-01: it holds that the indigent parent's statutory right to appointed counsel in a TPR includes the right to EFFECTIVE assistance, supplying the missing link between M.W./Joni B. (right to counsel) and Christopher D. (appellate counsel).

Added Dane County Department of Human Services v. Ponn P. (2005 WI 32) for OUT-02 and FAIL-01: it is the Wisconsin Supreme Court's decision on TPR no-contest pleas and the forfeiture or preservation of as-applied substantive due process challenges, and the immediate predecessor to Brenda B. Note the court styles it 'Ponn P.', not 'P.P.'

Added Waukesha County v. Steven H. (2000 WI 28) for DEC-05 and OUT-02: caution - the verifier described it as the leading abandonment case, but the opinion actually decides (1) that only the last out-of-home placement order before a TPR petition must carry the Wis. Stat. sec. 48.356(2) warning and (2) that sec. 48.422(3) requires the court to hear testimony supporting the petition's allegations, an error held harmless on this record. It is mapped for those two holdings, not for abandonment.

Added State v. Bobby G. (In re Marquette S.) (2007 WI 77) for DEC-03 and OUT-02: caution - the verifier described it as an as-applied substantive-due-process analysis, but the Wisconsin Supreme Court expressly resolved the case on statutory construction of Wis. Stat. sec. 48.415(6) and did not reach the constitutional question. It is therefore mapped to the grounds-proof nodes, not to FAIL-05.

Added Hernandez ex rel. Hernandez v. Foster (657 F.3d 463) for INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02: it is the Seventh Circuit's fullest treatment of the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment limits on removing and continuing to hold a child, and the case Xiong actually applies; it also holds that a parent's consent to a CPS safety plan may not be obtained through duress.

Added Siliven v. Indiana Dep't of Child Services (635 F.3d 921) for DEC-04: it states the operative question - probable cause to believe the child would be seriously endangered if not immediately removed - and requires that the removal's scope be limited to the exigency that justified it.

Added Darryl H. v. Coler (801 F.2d 893) for INP-08, INP-10 and DEC-02: it is the Seventh Circuit's foundational reasonableness framework for CPS investigative intrusions on a child's body, and the analytical framework Doe v. Heck expressly applies. It is a preliminary-posture decision (injunction denial affirmed; qualified immunity granted) and should be cited for the framework, not for a final constitutional ruling.

Added Michael C. v. Gresbach (526 F.3d 1008) for INP-08, DEC-02 and FAIL-02: it is the Wisconsin follow-on to Doe v. Heck, denying qualified immunity to a Bureau of Milwaukee Child Welfare caseworker who searched children at a private school, and holding that Wis. Stat. sec. 48.981(3)(c)1. and the agency's contrary policy did not make the search reasonable.

Added Dupuy v. Samuels (397 F.3d 493) for DEC-03 and DEC-02: it is the controlling circuit authority on procedural due process in administrative 'indicated'/substantiated findings and central-registry listings, and on the investigative standard that requires weighing exculpatory evidence. This fills the DEC-03 hole the prior brief flagged as unfilled.

Added Suter v. Artist M. (503 U.S. 347) for FAIL-03, ACT-02 and PMC-01: it holds as a matter of decision - not inference - that the Title IV-E 'reasonable efforts' requirement creates no privately enforceable right under sec. 1983, which is why federal performance standards are enforced through funding and oversight.

Added Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl (570 U.S. 637) for INP-11, ACT-04 and FAIL-05: it narrows 25 U.S.C. sec. 1912(d) and (f) where the parent never had legal or physical custody, and it postdates Luis R., which the prior brief conceded but did not cite around.

Added Haaland v. Brackeen (599 U.S. 255) for INP-11 and ACT-04: it rejects the Article I, anticommandeering, equal-protection and nondelegation attacks on ICWA and confirms the statute's continuing validity, which any current ICWA analysis for a Wisconsin county requires alongside the pre-2013 Wisconsin line.

Could not verify: none. All fourteen authorities named by the verifier were located on CourtListener in this session, their clusters and opinions retrieved, and their opinion text read; every one is real and on point, and all fourteen are included above.

Node-map rebalancing: the coverage rule caps each node at six cases, and four nodes were already at six before these additions. To seat the new authorities without exceeding the cap the following existing mappings were dropped, in each instance because the case is better served at a node it already occupies - DEC-03 lost Kelli B. (retained at FAIL-05) and Polashek (retained at INP-01/02/06/07, FAIL-06, PMC-05); OUT-02 lost Shirley E. and Brenda B. (both retained at FAIL-01); FAIL-01 lost Green County v. H.N. (retained at ACT-02, OUT-01, OUT-04, OUT-05) and T.H. v. La Crosse County (retained at DEC-05, OUT-04, OUT-05); DEC-05 lost Steven V. (retained at DEC-03, OUT-02) and W.A.B. (retained at INP-04, OUT-04). No case was orphaned. The 'relevance' objects of the pre-existing case entries were left unchanged as instructed, so a few of them still name a node the map no longer assigns them; where the two disagree, node_map governs.

Node-map consistency repairs made in this pass, using relevance already asserted by existing entries: INP-04 was carrying only W.A.B. although Joni B., M.W. and In re Peter B. each claim it, and now carries all four; INP-09 was carrying only Linzmeyer although In re Peter B. claims it, and now carries both; DEC-06 was carrying only Deegan although Sallie T. claims it, and now carries both; PMC-04 was carrying only DeShaney although In re Peter B. and Hammersley each claim it, and now carries all three. Every one of the 42 nodes now has between two and six cases.

This brief now carries 52 distinct cases, above the 20-to-40 per-jurisdiction guideline. The overage is deliberate: it is the cost of seating all fourteen leading authorities the verifier identified as missing, and every one of the 52 is mapped to at least one node.

Missing (for a later pass): State v. Margaret H., 2000 WI 42, 234 Wis. 2d 606, 610 N.W.2d 475 — the Wisconsin Supreme Court's leading statement on how a circuit court weighs the § 48.426(3) best-interests factors at the TPR dispositional phase, including the child's substitute-care bond and the weight (none required) to be given an adoptive resource's promise of continued contact with the birth family. The brief covers the disposition standard with Julie A.B. alone; Margaret H. is what practitioners actually argue at OUT-02 and OUT-03.

Missing (for a later pass): Brown County v. Shannon R., 2005 WI 160, 286 Wis. 2d 278, 706 N.W.2d 269 — holds the circuit court erred in refusing to let a parent present evidence at the TPR dispositional hearing. It is the dispositional-phase counterpart to C.L.K.'s grounds-phase structural-error holding and belongs at FAIL-01 and OUT-02, which currently carry no dispositional-phase reversal authority.

Missing (for a later pass): Walworth County Department of Health & Human Services v. Andrea L.O., 2008 WI 46, 309 Wis. 2d 161, 749 N.W.2d 168 — the Wisconsin Supreme Court's limiting companion to Jodie W., addressing when an incarcerated or otherwise constrained parent's failure to meet continuing-CHIPS conditions does and does not offend substantive due process. Citing Jodie W. at ACT-02, OUT-01 and FAIL-05 without Andrea L.O. materially overstates Jodie W.'s reach.

Missing (for a later pass): Woznicki v. Erickson, 202 Wis. 2d 178, 549 N.W.2d 699 (1996) — the Wisconsin Supreme Court decision requiring notice to the record subject and an opportunity to seek judicial review before a custodian releases records about that person. It is the necessary counterweight to Linzmeyer at PMC-05, INP-09 and FAIL-06; a brief that cites only Linzmeyer's 'strong presumption in favor of release' misstates Wisconsin open-records practice.

Missing (for a later pass): Lodl v. Progressive Northern Insurance Co., 2002 WI 71, 253 Wis. 2d 323, 646 N.W.2d 314 — the Wisconsin Supreme Court's controlling modern framework for § 893.80(4) governmental immunity and the ministerial-duty and known-danger exceptions. DEC-01, FAIL-02 and PMC-02 rest on Deegan, a 1994 court of appeals decision; Lodl is the current statement of the rule and of the exceptions that can defeat it.

Missing (for a later pass): C.L. v. Olson, 143 Wis. 2d 701, 422 N.W.2d 614 (1988) — the Wisconsin Supreme Court's known-danger exception to discretionary-act immunity for state human-services personnel. It is the principal Wisconsin route around the Deegan immunity bar at FAIL-02 and FAIL-04 and is absent entirely.
